Looking back at a week spent on a business system migration project, most of the pull requests I stacked up were tasks to "fix the slight differences between the newly written code and the original system." It wasn't about new features, nor was it about flashy refactoring. It was just a relentless repetition of "it was like this originally, so I'll fix it like this."
It's mundane. But within this mundanity, the essence of the migration work was entirely contained.
Migrating an old system to a new technology stack. It's a common project. The client's expectation is simple: "I want it to work just like it does now." This is where it gets tricky.
"Just like now" is not written in the specifications. What is written in the specifications is just a facade; the true specification is
the actual behavior of the currently running system

. What is returned when non-existent data is passed? How are fractional amounts rounded? Does deletion really remove the data, or does it just make it invisible? These "unwritten specifications" are exactly where the battle of migration is won or lost.

Working Examples and Patent Requirements
1. What are working examples?
What are working examples? There is no need to overthink it. In chemical patents, you can generally consider "working examples = experimental data" without any issues.
Working examples are mainly seen in chemical and biotechnology patents.

While they are familiar to those with experience in patent practice in these fields, it is actually not uncommon for patents in other technical fields to lack working examples accompanied by experimental data.
So, why are working examples important in chemical patents?
The reason is that in the fields of chemistry and biotechnology, it is often difficult to predict effects without actually conducting experiments.
